title: Replace a word in many files at once and keep .bak backups
summary: Find every file under a folder that contains the old text and replace it with the new text in place. Each changed file keeps its original as a .bak copy. Use it to rename a setting or a function across a project.

steps.explain: Preview first. grep -rn lists every line under DIR that contains the old text, with file name and line number. Nothing is changed.
steps.expect: Lines such as src/main.py:12:    old_name() with file, line number and text.

steps.explain: Replace the text. grep -rlZ lists the files that contain the old text, separated by zero bytes, so odd names are safe. xargs -0 -r passes them to sed, and -r does nothing if the list is empty. sed -i.bak edits each file and keeps the original as file.bak.
steps.expect: Usually no output. Each changed file now has a matching .bak copy next to it.

steps.explain: Check that the old text is gone from the real files. --exclude skips the .bak copies.
steps.expect: No output means no file still contains the old text. grep exits with status 1 in that case, which is not an error.

placeholders.name: OLD_TEXT
placeholders.description: The text that should be gone

rollback.explain: Put the backups back. Every X.bak file is moved over X, so the original text returns. Run it on the same folder.
rollback.cmd: find <DIR> -type f -name '*.bak' -exec sh -c 'for f; do mv -- "$f" "${f%.bak}"; done' sh {} +

warnings: The replacement changes every matching file under the folder. Check the preview step first.
The old text is a pattern: . * [ ] \ are special. Use a plain word, and never put a slash / in either text, because it ends the sed command early.
Rolling back with the .bak copies overwrites the changed files, so edits made after the replacement are lost.
